🚀 SPHEREX EXPLORER

Explore the sky. Investigate the universe.

SPHEREX EXPLORER is an astronomy platform for exploring planets, moons, asteroids, comets, stars, black holes and galaxies using scientific data.

Its special feature, COSMIC TIME MACHINE, will help users compare astronomical observations over time and investigate changes in the universe.

Our mission: Make space exploration and scientific discovery accessible to everyone. 🌌
summary: SphereX is an interactive web application built to make exploring astronomical data simple and accessible for everyone. To address the challenge, our platform allows users to enter specific sky coordinates and search across NASA's SPHEREx infrared data alongside multi-wavelength datasets and archives from other space agencies, such as ESA's Gaia and optical sky surveys. With a single click on the "Load Preview" button beneath any search result, users can immediately view visual image previews and corresponding cross-agency data for that region of the sky. This project is important because raw space telescope files often require complex scientific software to navigate. By bringing multiple international space datasets together in a clean, stress-free interface, SphereX empowers students, citizen scientists, and anyone curious about deep space to effortlessly explore the outer sky and spot celestial objects.
details:
What SphereX Does & How It Works

SphereX is a user-friendly web application built for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge that makes exploring vast astronomical datasets simple and stress-free. Users can enter specific sky coordinates into a clean search interface to query NASA's SPHEREx near-infrared archives alongside multi-wavelength data and catalogs from international space agencies and observatories—including ESA's Gaia DR3, NASA's WISE/NEOWISE and 2MASS, ZTF, DSS2, SDSS, Pan-STARRS, SIMBAD, NED, and JPL Horizons. Once search results appear, users can view the corresponding astronomical records and click the "Load Preview" button beneath any result to immediately render visual image previews of that sky region. Benefits & Intended Impact Raw astronomical data from space missions is often stored in massive, complex scientific formats (such as FITS cubes and TAP/SIA tables) that require specialized software and technical expertise to navigate. SphereX removes that barrier. Our intended impact is to democratize access to deep-sky observations so that students, educators, citizen scientists, and outer-space enthusiasts can effortlessly explore the cosmos, compare infrared and optical views, and spot interesting celestial objects without technical frustration.

Tools & Technologies Used • Development & Coding Environments: Antigravity and Visual Studio Code (VS Code) for building, structuring, and debugging the web application. • AI & Prototyping Assistants: Google AI Studio, Gemini, and ChatGPT to accelerate code generation, API integration, and interface refinement. • Data Services & APIs: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) SIAv2 and TAP services, HiPS sky survey tiles, ESA Gaia TAP services, and JPL/Minor Planet Center APIs. Creativity & Design Considerations What makes SphereX creative is how it unifies multi-agency, multi-wavelength space archives into a single, intuitive workflow designed for everyday users rather than just professional astrophysicists. While building the app, our team carefully considered several key factors:• Performance & Bandwidth: Instead of forcing the browser to download heavy astronomical image files all at once, we designed an on-demand "Load Preview" button so users only load visual imagery for the exact targets they want to inspect.

Our team utilized Super Intelligence (SI) tools—specifically Google AI Studio, Gemini, and ChatGPT—during the development phase to assist with writing and debugging code, structuring queries for astronomical archive APIs (such as NASA IRSA and ESA Gaia), and refining text documentation. All astronomical data and sky previews displayed in the application are sourced directly from official space agency archives, and no NASA logos, flags, or mission identifiers were generated or modified using SI tools.
